upcoming.title: Native Histograms
upcoming.description:
This milestone is mostly about merging the new native histograms (AKA sparse histograms AKA high-res histograms) into the main branch (and hide it behind a feature flag), and only after that about declaring native histograms a stable feature (ultimately no-op'ing the feature flag). Therefore, the priorities have a slightly different meaning (because the issues do not affect the released Prometheus versions before we merge to the main branch):
* **P0:** Prometheus, if built from the sparsehistogram branch, doesn't work properly until this is fixed.
* **P1:** We must fix this before merging to main (e.g. Prometheus might not work properly even if the feature flag is not set)
* **P2:** We can merge to main without this but we need to fix this to declare Histograms stable.
* **P3:** Nice to have. Can be introduced later without a breaking change.
* **P4:** The future! Do not focus on this for now. (Labeled as Pmaybe.)

signals.title: Compactions cause the configured storage.tsdb.retention.size to be exceeded (and risk of running out of disk space)
signals.text: ## Excerpt / TL;DR The set limit of storage to be used (`storage.tsdb.retention.size`) is violated during compaction which poses a the risk of running out of disk space. The reason is that Prometheus does not take into account the required space for the temporary blocks. See **Proposal** section for two suggested approaches to fix this and allow Prometheus to reliably avoid exceeding it's allowance. ## Issue The `storage.tsdb.retention.size` option (https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/storage/#operational-aspects) was a great addition to allow keeping metrics in relation to the available storage. While this can be a provisioned volume from some cloud provider or a LVM volume or just the amount of space you can give to Prometheus and then have it make the most of the available space (https://www.robustperception.io/configuring-prometheus-storage-retention/). While there were some issues with WAL files and head_chunks not counted against the configured limit, those are now all taken into account when determining the current storage size thus reducing confusion for users and the risk of running out of disk space. Since checkpoints and first level of compactions happen over relatively small time intervals of two hours the peak is relatively small and usually just about keeping some sensible head room for - just as written in the documentation: > So the minimum requirement for the disk is the peak space taken by the wal (the WAL and Checkpoint) and chunks_head (m-mapped Head chunks) directory combined (peaks every 2 hours) There also is good documentation on how to calculate the space requirements regarding the amount of samples ingested per time interval and their average size via built-in metrics: * https://www.robustperception.io/how-much-disk-space-do-prometheus-blocks-use/ * https://www.robustperception.io/how-much-space-does-the-wal-take-up/ Even though this all helps to anticipate how man samples and time series can be stored and over which retention times using the available space, more critical to the risk of running out of space are the compactions over longer periods covering up to 31 days of samples by default (https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/storage/#compaction). The leveled compaction time ranges and the compaction is nicely explained at leveled compaction: https://ganeshvernekar.com/blog/prometheus-tsdb-compaction-and-retention/#condition-2-preset-time-ranges. And there also is documentation at https://www.robustperception.io/configuring-prometheus-storage-retention/ explaining the requirement to keep enough space for such compactions: > As of Prometheus [2.7](https://www.robustperception.io/new-features-in-prometheus-2-7-0) and 2.8 there's new flags and options. 2.7 introduced an option for size-based retention with --storage.tsdb.retention.size, that is specifying a maximum amount of disk space used by blocks. This is still a bit best effort though as it does not (yet) include the space taken by the WAL or blocks being populated by compaction. **To be safe allow for space for the WAL and one maximum size block (which is the smaller of 10% of the retention time and a month).** This is simply because the compaction only marks blocks as `Deletable` (https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/e51a17b50159d397544d7f62775ee9ceaf48cfc8/tsdb/compact.go#L71), but requires the additional storage to first write the merged blocks. Coming to the real issue for me, this is not easy to convert into an actual amount of space to subtract from the total available space when setting `storage.tsdb.retention.size` aiming to maximize the storage retention time and making the most use of the space there is, see https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/10287. And even if I would use the referenced metrics to calculate the size a directory holding 31d worth of samples has now, this clearly is changing over time with time series churn or just more time series being ingested. And while the metrics are there in Prometheus, it's still not something that works without manual interventions and adjustments. This might be the cause for the issues like https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/10890. To me, the current complexity in setting up retention by storage size beats the purpose of having a _set it and forget it_ setting which translates to: _Only use X GB of storage and make the most of it._ If I have to calculate the ingest rate and bytes per month and continuously monitor and adjust for that ... I could just end up converting this to a suitable retention TIME instead beating the purpose of having a retention size setting in the first place. ## Proposal I therefore propose to add functionality to not exceed `storage.tsdb.retention.size` during compactions. 1. Maybe this could be done by extending on the existing compaction planning to calculate a worse-case of storage required to write the new merged blocks. This value could be added to the "used storage" just like the current size of the WAL was added via https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/5886. 2. Another approach would be to make the compaction have a smaller footprint altogether by continuously removing the blocks from the previous compaction level and not having all block of two compaction levels exist in parallel. This would then define an upper bound for the amount of additional storage required - something similar to the documented space requirements for WAL and their checkpoints. By tackling this issue, it would be come MUCH less likely to run Prometheus into out of space ... which still happens when currently using `retention.size` feature (https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/8884).

signals.title: Label API is much slower than equivalent series API
signals.text: ### What did you do? We have a metric called `colo_metadata` with `colo_name` as one of the labels. I'm interested in getting all the values of the label for Grafana reasons. Querying this via labels API is ridiculously slow: ``` $ for i in $(seq 1 3); do time curl -s "http://localhost:3000/api/v1/label/colo_name/values?match%5B%5D=colo_metadata&start=$(date +%s | awk '{ print $1 - 3600 * 24 * 7 }')&end=$(date +%s)" | jq .data[] | sort | uniq | wc -l; done 640 real 0m29.146s user 0m0.047s sys 0m0.014s 640 real 0m28.510s user 0m0.046s sys 0m0.018s 640 real 0m30.322s user 0m0.043s sys 0m0.015s ``` Doing the exact same thing by querying the series API is fast: ``` $ for i in $(seq 1 3); do time curl -s "http://localhost:3000/api/v1/series?match%5B%5D=colo_metadata&start=$(date +%s | awk '{ print $1 - 3600 * 24 }')&end=$(date +%s)" | jq .data[].colo_name | sort | uniq -c | wc -l; done 638 real 0m0.057s user 0m0.059s sys 0m0.011s 638 real 0m0.057s user 0m0.057s sys 0m0.013s 638 real 0m0.055s user 0m0.054s sys 0m0.014s ``` ### What did you expect to see? Labels API is at least as fast as series API. ### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances? Labels API is excruciatingly slow. ### System information Linux 6.6.41-cloudflare-2024.7.6 ### Prometheus version ```text prometheus, version 2.53.0 (branch: master, revision: 774cb1fad4cc043824538fc8a2354c2bcf59f4b8) build user: builder@k8s-pdx-c-managed-h7bgt build date: 20240620-12:36:39 go version: go1.22.4 platform: linux/amd64 tags: netgo,builtinassets,stringlabels ``` ### Prometheus configuration file _No response_ ### Alertmanager version _No response_ ### Alertmanager configuration file _No response_ ### Logs _No response_

signals.title: `promtool check config` ignores `--enable-feature` flags for PromQL experimental features
signals.text: ### What happened After the parser refactoring in #17977, `promtool check config` no longer respects `--enable-feature` flags for PromQL experimental features (e.g. `promql-experimental-functions`, `promql-extended-range-selectors`). ### Root cause In `cmd/promtool/main.go`, the `CheckConfig` function creates a default parser with no features enabled: ```go // cmd/promtool/main.go:622 rulesFailed, rulesHaveErrors := checkRules(ruleFiles, lintSettings.rulesLintConfig, parser.NewParser(parser.Options{})) ``` Before #17977, this code path called `parser.ParseExpr()` which read global flags that were set earlier in `main()`. Now that globals are replaced with per-instance options, this call site uses a fresh parser that ignores the user's feature flags stored in `promtoolParserOpts`. ### Expected behavior `promtool check config --enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions myconfig.yml` should accept rules using experimental PromQL functions. ### Actual behavior Rules using experimental PromQL functions are rejected with parse errors, even when the corresponding `--enable-feature` flag is passed. ### Fix Pass `promtoolParser` (or accept it as a parameter) instead of `parser.NewParser(parser.Options{})`.

signals.title: `promtool test rules` ignores `--enable-feature` flags when loading rule files
signals.text: ### What happened After the parser refactoring in #17977, `promtool test rules` no longer respects `--enable-feature` flags when loading rule files containing experimental PromQL syntax. ### Root cause In `cmd/promtool/unittest.go`, the `testGroup.test()` method creates a `rules.ManagerOptions` without setting the `Parser` field: ```go // cmd/promtool/unittest.go:252-258 opts := &rules.ManagerOptions{ QueryFunc: rules.EngineQueryFunc(suite.QueryEngine(), suite.Storage()), Appendable: suite.Storage(), Context: context.Background(), NotifyFunc: func(context.Context, string, ...*rules.Alert) {}, Logger: promslog.NewNopLogger(), // Parser field is missing } ``` The `rules.NewManager` then falls back to `parser.NewParser(parser.Options{})`, which has no experimental features enabled. Meanwhile, `tg.parser` (which does have the correct features) is only used for parsing expected samples (lines 485, 489) but not for loading the actual rule files. Before #17977, the global `parser.EnableExperimentalFunctions` (etc.) was set in `main()` and respected by all `parser.ParseExpr` calls, including those inside the rules manager. ### Expected behavior `promtool test rules --enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions test.yml` should load rule files that use experimental PromQL functions. ### Actual behavior Rule files using experimental PromQL functions fail to load with parse errors. ### Fix Add `Parser: tg.parser` to the `rules.ManagerOptions` struct initialization.

signals.title: otlptranslator: valid OTLP histogram stored with le="+Inf" below its own _count
signals.text: ### What did you do? On `main` at `44d6a0e0b`, translated a classic `HistogramDataPoint` whose explicit bounds end at `+Inf`, then read back its series: ```go pt.SetCount(42) pt.SetSum(100) pt.BucketCounts().FromRaw([]uint64{5, 10, 20, 7}) pt.ExplicitBounds().FromRaw([]float64{1, 2, math.Inf(1)}) ``` This data point satisfies every MUST the proto states for it: `bucket_counts` is one longer than `explicit_bounds`, the bounds are strictly increasing, and `count` equals their sum (`5 + 10 + 20 + 7 = 42`). ### What did you expect to see? `le="+Inf"` equal to `_count`, as the cumulative convention requires. ### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances? Two totals, disagreeing. `_count` is `42` and `le="+Inf"` is `35`, so the stored histogram answers differently depending on which series is read, and nothing reports it: the input broke no MUST, the bucket series is still monotonic, and no error is returned. **The same input is rejected on the other path.** With `convert_histograms_to_nhcb: true` the identical data point becomes ``` {count:42, sum:100, [-Inf,1]:5, (1,2]:10, (2,+Inf]:20, (+Inf,+Inf]:7} ``` and `histogram.Validate()` refuses it: ``` custom buckets: last +Inf bound must not be explicitly defined: histogram custom bounds must be finite ``` That rule is `model/histogram/generic.go:566`, and `tsdb/head_append.go:828` turns it into a rejected sample. It also looks deliberate rather than incidental: #17320 revisited that function to accept `-Inf` and kept `+Inf` rejected. So the invariant is already stated here, an explicit `+Inf` bound must not be defined, and the classic path is the one that does not hold to it — while being the default, since `convert_histograms_to_nhcb` is absent from `DefaultOTLPConfig`. **Where the second `le="+Inf"` comes from.** The loop over explicit bounds writes one `_bucket` series per bound, formatting the bound into `le` (`helper.go:308-337`), so the `+Inf` bound emits `le="+Inf"` carrying the cumulative count at that point, `35`. Then `le="+Inf"` is synthesized again from `pt.Count()` (`helper.go:340-346`). Both reach `Append` with identical labels and timestamp. Both are accepted and the commit keeps the first: two appends of `35` then `42` at the same timestamp in one batch return no error and store `35`, while the same second append issued after a commit is refused with `duplicate sample for timestamp 1000; overrides not allowed: existing 35, new value 99`. The fourth bucket count, `7`, is the overflow bucket, which this path never reads. **A test that shows it.** Fails on `main`, passes with the change: ``` --- FAIL: TestPrometheusConverter_ExplicitInfBoundDoesNotReplaceCount (0.00s) Messages: le="+Inf" was written more than once ``` **How often this happens — my guess is rarely, and here is the reasoning.** I have not counted producers. The schema makes an explicit `+Inf` bound unnecessary: `bucket_counts` must be one longer than `explicit_bounds`, so the last count already means "above the last bound". An SDK following that shape has no reason to emit one, which leaves translators from formats where `+Inf` is explicit, a Prometheus classic histogram round-tripping through OTLP being the obvious case. So I would expect this to be uncommon. It still seemed worth reporting, because the input is valid, the loss is silent, and the guard is one condition. A PR follows with the change and the test above. /cc @beorn7, who kept the explicit `+Inf` bound rejected in #17320, and @ArthurSens for `otlptranslator`. ### Prometheus version ```text prometheus, version (branch: main, revision: 44d6a0e0b1dbdcba4e68853d50e0bafc87d90507) build user: build date: go version: go1.26.1 platform: darwin/arm64 tags: unknown ```

signals.title: promtool: no tool to find inconsistent classic histograms in a TSDB
signals.text: ### Proposal Quantiles, alerts and recording rules can be computed from classic histograms whose stored buckets contradict each other — and nothing lists which series are affected, or since when. **How the data gets there.** No ingest path cross-checks the float series of a classic histogram: scrape, remote write and the OTLP receiver append what was sent. Buckets whose cumulative counts decrease, or a `le="+Inf"` bucket disagreeing with `_count`, are stored as-is. Native histograms are rejected at append (`model/histogram/histogram.go:474`, `ErrHistogramCountMismatch`); classic ones have no equivalent check anywhere. **What it costs while it sits there.** `histogram_quantile` repairs non-monotonic input on the fly (`util/annotations/annotations.go:163`) and keeps returning plausible numbers, so SLOs and alerts built on an affected histogram are computed from silently patched data. The only signal is a per-query info annotation, phrased as a property of the query — the data stays broken for every next query. That annotation had to be taught to at least name the affected metric (#15411); finding all affected series in a TSDB still has no tool. **The fix.** `promtool tsdb check-histograms [db path]` scans a TSDB range (`--min-time`/`--max-time`) and reports, per histogram: non-monotonic cumulative buckets; `le="+Inf"` disagreeing with `_count`; `le` labels that do not parse as a float (`le="NaN"` is storable today); duplicate `le` spellings carrying different values at the same timestamp (`le="1"` vs `le="1.0"` on disjoint timestamps — the v3 migration shape — is recognized as clean); histograms with no `+Inf` bucket at all. Exits non-zero when anything is found, so it can run from cron or CI. Placed under `promtool tsdb` because it takes a database path like `dump` and `analyze` (`promtool check` takes config files and server URLs), and marked `[Experimental]` like `dump-openmetrics`. **Limits.** Native histograms are out of scope — already validated at append. And I have not measured how often such data occurs in the wild — this tool is how an operator answers that for their own TSDB. Found and verified on `main` at `44d6a0e`; file and line references are against that commit. cc @dgl — promtool is your path, and this proposes a new subcommand in it.

signals.title: scrape: synthesize start times for summary _sum and _count series
signals.text: Motivation: Start-timestamp (ST) auto-synthesis was implemented for all cumulative counter-like series on the scrape path, but summary types were left out: their _sum and _count series (which have counter semantics) did not get a synthesized start time. This was tracked by an in-code TODO and called out by maintainers as the remaining gap for #14763. Approach: Extend checkAndSynthesizeStartTime to handle model.MetricTypeSummary. A summary family exposes cumulative _sum and _count series alongside gauge-like quantile series, so only the _sum and _count series may be synthesized. signals.title: tsdb: release oversized head-chunk cache for single-chunk series
signals.text: Range-query and compaction readers cache collected head chunks for sequential access. signals.title: Avoid locking HEAD shards when running gc
signals.text: After HEAD writes a block it runs GC to prune series that no longer have any chunks in HEAD, this fully locks each HEAD shard while it's being scanned for series to prune. That locked shard blocks all queries (because it's a write lock) and it can be visible on metrics as a sudden spike in queued queries. The more series we have in Prometheus the more visible this is. Often there are very few series to actually prune, so most of this time is spent iterating over all series, the more series the longer each shard scan takes (since the number of shards is static). Try to avoid this blocking by doing prunes in two phases: - first iterate under a read lock and find series to prune - then, if there are any series found, do a second loop over identified series and prune these under a write lock This way we only lock each shard to the actual pruning, not for scanning. It's safe because series can only receive samples, they can't become empty, while we're running a GC. <!-- - Please give your PR a title in the form "area: short description". signals.title: otlptranslator: keep le="+Inf" equal to count when a bound is +Inf
signals.text: Previously, an OTLP histogram whose `explicit_bounds` end at `+Inf` produced two `le="+Inf"` samples for the same series and timestamp: one from the loop over explicit bounds, carrying the cumulative count at that bound, and one synthesized from `pt.Count()`. Both appends succeed, because a duplicate at the same timestamp is rejected across appender batches and not within one, and the commit keeps the first. So `le="+Inf"` ended up holding a bucket total while `_count` held the count. This skips an infinite bound in the loop and lets the synthesized bucket carry the count: ```go if math.IsInf(bound, 1) { continue } ``` `explicit_bounds` is required to be strictly increasing, so in conforming input `+Inf` is the last bound and no later bucket depends on the skipped iteration. The bound's exemplars still reach the synthesized bucket through the remainder assigned after the loop, so no exemplar is dropped. No existing fixture in the package sets an infinite bound, so the guard does not change any current output. The NHCB path already refuses the same input: `histogram.Validate()` rejects an explicitly defined `+Inf` bound at `model/histogram/generic.go:566`, and #17320 kept that while relaxing `-Inf`. This brings the classic path into line with it. `TestPrometheusConverter_ExplicitInfBoundDoesNotReplaceCount` fails on `main` with `le="+Inf" was written more than once` and passes with the change. #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: Fixes #19424 #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). *Reviewers should verify clarity and quality.* ```release-notes [BUGFIX] OTLP: Keep `le="+Inf"` equal to the data point count when explicit bounds end at `+Inf`. ```

signals.title: tsdb: reserve disk space before block compaction
signals.text: #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: Fixes #11112 #### What does this PR do? Size-based retention currently runs after a compacted block has been written, while both the source blocks and their replacement are still on disk. This allows compaction to temporarily exceed the configured retention limit. Before compacting on-disk blocks, this change reserves space equal to the planned source blocks. If the retained data plus that reservation exceeds the configured fixed-size or percentage limit, the existing retention policy removes the oldest blocks through `reloadBlocks` and the compaction is replanned. The reservation is only applied with the default block deletion policy. Downstream users that provide a custom `BlocksToDelete` callback retain the existing behavior. No exported API or configuration surface is changed. When size-based retention is disabled, compaction follows the existing path without additional retention work. Tests cover: * Fixed-size and percentage retention reservations. * Custom block deletion policy compatibility. * Peak on-disk usage during a real leveled compaction. Verification: * Focused and adjacent TSDB tests. * Focused regression tests with the race detector. * Signed commit and clean diff checks. #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). *Reviewers should verify clarity and quality.* ```release-notes [BUGFIX] TSDB: Reserve disk space for replacement blocks before compaction when size-based retention is enabled. ```

signals.title: otlptranslator: make the histogram_1 test fixture OTLP-conforming
signals.text: `TestFromMetrics`'s `histogram_1` fixture sets `count` to 15 with `bucket_counts` of `{3, 11, 0}`, which sum to 14. OTLP requires the two to agree, and the native-histogram expectation the test asserts inherits the mismatch — handed to `histogram.Validate`, that expected value is refused: ``` 14 observations found in buckets, but the Count field is 15: histogram's observation count should equal the number of observations found in the buckets (in absence of NaN) ``` The declared `sum` of 155 settles which side is wrong: 14 observations at or below the last bound of 1.123 cannot sum to more than 15.8, so at least one observation belongs in the `(1.123, +Inf]` overflow bucket. The first commit sets that bucket to 1. It is not emitted as a `_bucket` series, so the classic expectations are unchanged; only the native-histogram delta moves, from `-11` to `-10`. The second commit checks the property instead of the number: every expected native histogram in that block goes through `Validate` before the comparison, so an expectation the appender would reject fails the test. Reverting the first commit while keeping the second makes `TestFromMetrics/successful/convertHistogramsToNHCB=true` fail. The check is scoped to that block. `TestTemporality`'s expectations come from an exponential data point with `count=1` and no buckets, which is a question about that input rather than about the expectation. #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: None. #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). *Reviewers should verify clarity and quality.* ```release-notes NONE ```

signals.title: promql: fix panic in extendFloats on a series with an empty window
signals.text: `extendFloats` dereferences `floats[len(floats)-1]` with no emptiness check, and `matrixSelector` calls it for every series the querier returned. A series can be returned and then trimmed to nothing — selection is per chunk, trimming is per sample — so a chunk that *spans* the query window without holding a sample inside it yields an empty slice: ``` demo_metric[10s] -> 200, matrix, 0 series demo_metric[10s] anchored -> 422 unexpected error: runtime error: index out of range [-1] demo_metric[10s] smoothed -> 422 unexpected error: runtime error: index out of range [0] with length 0 ``` Two messages from one hole: `anchored` leaves the index at `len-1` == -1 (Go omits the length suffix for a negative index), `smoothed` recomputes it as `sort.Search(-1, …)` == 0. Any scrape gap longer than `range + lookbackDelta` reaches this when queried inside the gap, since the modifiers widen the sample window by `lookbackDelta`; reproduced against the released `prom/prometheus:v3.13.2` image by killing a real target for 40s. The panic is recovered, so this is a 422 and a logged stack trace per attempt, not a crash. **The fix** returns the empty slice before indexing, as-is rather than a fresh `[]FPoint{}` so the caller can still pool it. That matches #17479, which fixed `resets`/`changes` to return empty for anchored selectors when the samples are outside the range. `extendFloats` has exactly two callers, both in `matrixSelector`, so this is the whole reachable surface — `rate(foo[2m] anchored)` goes through `extendedRate` and was already correct. Whether such a series should reach `matrixSelector` at all is a larger question this PR does not touch. **Tests:** five `promqltest` cases in `extended_vectors.test` — the two panicking queries, the no-modifier control, and two asserting extension still produces the right values when the window does contain samples. The two panic cases were confirmed to fail on an unpatched tree. #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: <!-- No issue filed; reported directly as this PR. --> #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). ```release-notes [BUGFIX] PromQL: Fix a panic in range selectors using the experimental `anchored` or `smoothed` modifier when the selected series has no samples inside the query window, for example a query evaluated inside a scrape gap. ```

This attack allows for a malicious GOPROXY to serve malicious module content that cannot be detected by evaluating the transparency log. All tiles are now correctly verified against their parents. signal.title: `promtool check config` ignores `--enable-feature` flags for PromQL experimental features
signal.text: ### What happened After the parser refactoring in #17977, `promtool check config` no longer respects `--enable-feature` flags for PromQL experimental features (e.g. `promql-experimental-functions`, `promql-extended-range-selectors`). ### Root cause In `cmd/promtool/main.go`, the `CheckConfig` function creates a default parser with no features enabled: ```go // cmd/promtool/main.go:622 rulesFailed, rulesHaveErrors := checkRules(ruleFiles, lintSettings.rulesLintConfig, parser.NewParser(parser.Options{})) ``` Before #17977, this code path called `parser.ParseExpr()` which read global flags that were set earlier in `main()`. Now that globals are replaced with per-instance options, this call site uses a fresh parser that ignores the user's feature flags stored in `promtoolParserOpts`. ### Expected behavior `promtool check config --enable-feature=promql-experimental-functions myconfig.yml` should accept rules using experimental PromQL functions. ### Actual behavior Rules using experimental PromQL functions are rejected with parse errors, even when the corresponding `--enable-feature` flag is passed. ### Fix Pass `promtoolParser` (or accept it as a parameter) instead of `parser.NewParser(parser.Options{})`.

signal.title: `promtool test rules` ignores `--enable-feature` flags when loading rule files
signal.text: ### What happened After the parser refactoring in #17977, `promtool test rules` no longer respects `--enable-feature` flags when loading rule files containing experimental PromQL syntax. ### Root cause In `cmd/promtool/unittest.go`, the `testGroup.test()` method creates a `rules.ManagerOptions` without setting the `Parser` field: ```go // cmd/promtool/unittest.go:252-258 opts := &rules.ManagerOptions{ QueryFunc: rules.EngineQueryFunc(suite.QueryEngine(), suite.Storage()), Appendable: suite.Storage(), Context: context.Background(), NotifyFunc: func(context.Context, string, ...*rules.Alert) {}, Logger: promslog.NewNopLogger(), // Parser field is missing } ``` The `rules.NewManager` then falls back to `parser.NewParser(parser.Options{})`, which has no experimental features enabled. signal.title: promql: fix panic in extendFloats on a series with an empty window
signal.text: `extendFloats` dereferences `floats[len(floats)-1]` with no emptiness check, and `matrixSelector` calls it for every series the querier returned. A series can be returned and then trimmed to nothing — selection is per chunk, trimming is per sample — so a chunk that *spans* the query window without holding a sample inside it yields an empty slice: ``` demo_metric[10s] -> 200, matrix, 0 series demo_metric[10s] anchored -> 422 unexpected error: runtime error: index out of range [-1] demo_metric[10s] smoothed -> 422 unexpected error: runtime error: index out of range [0] with length 0 ``` Two messages from one hole: `anchored` leaves the index at `len-1` == -1 (Go omits the length suffix for a negative index), `smoothed` recomputes it as `sort.Search(-1, …)` == 0. Any scrape gap longer than `range + lookbackDelta` reaches this when queried inside the gap, since the modifiers widen the sample window by `lookbackDelta`; reproduced against the released `prom/prometheus:v3.13.2` image by killing a real target for 40s. The panic is recovered, so this is a 422 and a logged stack trace per attempt, not a crash. **The fix** returns the empty slice before indexing, as-is rather than a fresh `[]FPoint{}` so the caller can still pool it. That matches #17479, which fixed `resets`/`changes` to return empty for anchored selectors when the samples are outside the range. `extendFloats` has exactly two callers, both in `matrixSelector`, so this is the whole reachable surface — `rate(foo[2m] anchored)` goes through `extendedRate` and was already correct. Whether such a series should reach `matrixSelector` at all is a larger question this PR does not touch. **Tests:** five `promqltest` cases in `extended_vectors.test` — the two panicking queries, the no-modifier control, and two asserting extension still produces the right values when the window does contain samples. The two panic cases were confirmed to fail on an unpatched tree. #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: <!-- No issue filed; reported directly as this PR. --> #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). ```release-notes [BUGFIX] PromQL: Fix a panic in range selectors using the experimental `anchored` or `smoothed` modifier when the selected series has no samples inside the query window, for example a query evaluated inside a scrape gap. ```

signal.title: tsdb: release oversized head-chunk cache for single-chunk series
signal.text: Range-query and compaction readers cache collected head chunks for sequential access. When a reader moved from a series with more than `headChunksBufMaxCap` head chunks to a different series with zero or one head chunk, the direct-lookup fast path returned before applying the capacity policy. The reader then retained the oversized backing array and its chunk pointers until it closed or visited another multi-chunk series. Release the oversized cache on that series switch, resetting the fingerprint and slice together. Preserve the backing array for the same series so it can still be reused after mmap or truncation. The cache-cap regression now covers both multi-chunk and single-chunk destinations and verifies that caching can repopulate after the release. <details> <summary>Benchstat</summary> Compared base `44d6a0e0b` with head `da183769b` using Go 1.26.6 on Darwin/ARM64 with an Apple M4 Pro. The temporary harness enabled the cache with `SelectHints.Step = 15s`; six samples per revision were interleaved and order-balanced. | Cache-enabled benchmark | Base | Head | Result | | --- | ---: | ---: | --- | | `HeadChunkQuerier/multi_chunk` | 377.4µs | 379.5µs | No significant change (`p=0.310`) | | `HeadChunkQuerier/single_chunk` | 36.36µs | 36.63µs | No significant change (`p=0.394`) | | `HeadQuerier/multi_chunk` | 842.9µs | 861.0µs | +2.15% (`p=0.015`); not reproduced | | `HeadQuerier/single_chunk` | 28.00µs | 28.39µs | No significant change (`p=0.394`) | The initial `HeadQuerier/multi_chunk` result did not reproduce in a fresh six-sample confirmation (846.3µs base versus 845.5µs head, `p=0.310`); its cache-disabled control was also unchanged. signal.title: otlptranslator: make the histogram_1 test fixture OTLP-conforming
signal.text: `TestFromMetrics`'s `histogram_1` fixture sets `count` to 15 with `bucket_counts` of `{3, 11, 0}`, which sum to 14. OTLP requires the two to agree, and the native-histogram expectation the test asserts inherits the mismatch — handed to `histogram.Validate`, that expected value is refused: ``` 14 observations found in buckets, but the Count field is 15: histogram's observation count should equal the number of observations found in the buckets (in absence of NaN) ``` The declared `sum` of 155 settles which side is wrong: 14 observations at or below the last bound of 1.123 cannot sum to more than 15.8, so at least one observation belongs in the `(1.123, +Inf]` overflow bucket. The first commit sets that bucket to 1. It is not emitted as a `_bucket` series, so the classic expectations are unchanged; only the native-histogram delta moves, from `-11` to `-10`. The second commit checks the property instead of the number: every expected native histogram in that block goes through `Validate` before the comparison, so an expectation the appender would reject fails the test. Reverting the first commit while keeping the second makes `TestFromMetrics/successful/convertHistogramsToNHCB=true` fail. The check is scoped to that block. `TestTemporality`'s expectations come from an exponential data point with `count=1` and no buckets, which is a question about that input rather than about the expectation. #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: None. #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). *Reviewers should verify clarity and quality.* ```release-notes NONE ```

signal.title: Compactions cause the configured storage.tsdb.retention.size to be exceeded (and risk of running out of disk space)
signal.text: ## Excerpt / TL;DR The set limit of storage to be used (`storage.tsdb.retention.size`) is violated during compaction which poses a the risk of running out of disk space. The reason is that Prometheus does not take into account the required space for the temporary blocks. See **Proposal** section for two suggested approaches to fix this and allow Prometheus to reliably avoid exceeding it's allowance. ## Issue The `storage.tsdb.retention.size` option (https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/storage/#operational-aspects) was a great addition to allow keeping metrics in relation to the available storage. While this can be a provisioned volume from some cloud provider or a LVM volume or just the amount of space you can give to Prometheus and then have it make the most of the available space (https://www.robustperception.io/configuring-prometheus-storage-retention/). While there were some issues with WAL files and head_chunks not counted against the configured limit, those are now all taken into account when determining the current storage size thus reducing confusion for users and the risk of running out of disk space. Since checkpoints and first level of compactions happen over relatively small time intervals of two hours the peak is relatively small and usually just about keeping some sensible head room for - just as written in the documentation: > So the minimum requirement for the disk is the peak space taken by the wal (the WAL and Checkpoint) and chunks_head (m-mapped Head chunks) directory combined (peaks every 2 hours) There also is good documentation on how to calculate the space requirements regarding the amount of samples ingested per time interval and their average size via built-in metrics: * https://www.robustperception.io/how-much-disk-space-do-prometheus-blocks-use/ * https://www.robustperception.io/how-much-space-does-the-wal-take-up/ Even though this all helps to anticipate how man samples and time series can be stored and over which retention times using the available space, more critical to the risk of running out of space are the compactions over longer periods covering up to 31 days of samples by default (https://prometheus.io/docs/prometheus/latest/storage/#compaction). The leveled compaction time ranges and the compaction is nicely explained at leveled compaction: https://ganeshvernekar.com/blog/prometheus-tsdb-compaction-and-retention/#condition-2-preset-time-ranges. And there also is documentation at https://www.robustperception.io/configuring-prometheus-storage-retention/ explaining the requirement to keep enough space for such compactions: > As of Prometheus [2.7](https://www.robustperception.io/new-features-in-prometheus-2-7-0) and 2.8 there's new flags and options. 2.7 introduced an option for size-based retention with --storage.tsdb.retention.size, that is specifying a maximum amount of disk space used by blocks. This is still a bit best effort though as it does not (yet) include the space taken by the WAL or blocks being populated by compaction. **To be safe allow for space for the WAL and one maximum size block (which is the smaller of 10% of the retention time and a month).** This is simply because the compaction only marks blocks as `Deletable` (https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/blob/e51a17b50159d397544d7f62775ee9ceaf48cfc8/tsdb/compact.go#L71), but requires the additional storage to first write the merged blocks. Coming to the real issue for me, this is not easy to convert into an actual amount of space to subtract from the total available space when setting `storage.tsdb.retention.size` aiming to maximize the storage retention time and making the most use of the space there is, see https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/10287. And even if I would use the referenced metrics to calculate the size a directory holding 31d worth of samples has now, this clearly is changing over time with time series churn or just more time series being ingested. And while the metrics are there in Prometheus, it's still not something that works without manual interventions and adjustments. This might be the cause for the issues like https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/10890. To me, the current complexity in setting up retention by storage size beats the purpose of having a _set it and forget it_ setting which translates to: _Only use X GB of storage and make the most of it._ If I have to calculate the ingest rate and bytes per month and continuously monitor and adjust for that ... I could just end up converting this to a suitable retention TIME instead beating the purpose of having a retention size setting in the first place. ## Proposal I therefore propose to add functionality to not exceed `storage.tsdb.retention.size` during compactions. 1. Maybe this could be done by extending on the existing compaction planning to calculate a worse-case of storage required to write the new merged blocks. This value could be added to the "used storage" just like the current size of the WAL was added via https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/pull/5886. 2. Another approach would be to make the compaction have a smaller footprint altogether by continuously removing the blocks from the previous compaction level and not having all block of two compaction levels exist in parallel. This would then define an upper bound for the amount of additional storage required - something similar to the documented space requirements for WAL and their checkpoints. By tackling this issue, it would be come MUCH less likely to run Prometheus into out of space ... which still happens when currently using `retention.size` feature (https://github.com/prometheus/prometheus/issues/8884).

signal.title: tsdb: reserve disk space before block compaction
signal.text: #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: Fixes #11112 #### What does this PR do? Size-based retention currently runs after a compacted block has been written, while both the source blocks and their replacement are still on disk. This allows compaction to temporarily exceed the configured retention limit. Before compacting on-disk blocks, this change reserves space equal to the planned source blocks. If the retained data plus that reservation exceeds the configured fixed-size or percentage limit, the existing retention policy removes the oldest blocks through `reloadBlocks` and the compaction is replanned. The reservation is only applied with the default block deletion policy. Downstream users that provide a custom `BlocksToDelete` callback retain the existing behavior. No exported API or configuration surface is changed. When size-based retention is disabled, compaction follows the existing path without additional retention work. Tests cover: * Fixed-size and percentage retention reservations. * Custom block deletion policy compatibility. * Peak on-disk usage during a real leveled compaction. Verification: * Focused and adjacent TSDB tests. * Focused regression tests with the race detector. * Signed commit and clean diff checks. #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). *Reviewers should verify clarity and quality.* ```release-notes [BUGFIX] TSDB: Reserve disk space for replacement blocks before compaction when size-based retention is enabled. ```

signal.title: promtool: no tool to find inconsistent classic histograms in a TSDB
signal.text: ### Proposal Quantiles, alerts and recording rules can be computed from classic histograms whose stored buckets contradict each other — and nothing lists which series are affected, or since when. **How the data gets there.** No ingest path cross-checks the float series of a classic histogram: scrape, remote write and the OTLP receiver append what was sent. Buckets whose cumulative counts decrease, or a `le="+Inf"` bucket disagreeing with `_count`, are stored as-is. Native histograms are rejected at append (`model/histogram/histogram.go:474`, `ErrHistogramCountMismatch`); classic ones have no equivalent check anywhere. **What it costs while it sits there.** `histogram_quantile` repairs non-monotonic input on the fly (`util/annotations/annotations.go:163`) and keeps returning plausible numbers, so SLOs and alerts built on an affected histogram are computed from silently patched data. The only signal is a per-query info annotation, phrased as a property of the query — the data stays broken for every next query. That annotation had to be taught to at least name the affected metric (#15411); finding all affected series in a TSDB still has no tool. **The fix.** `promtool tsdb check-histograms [db path]` scans a TSDB range (`--min-time`/`--max-time`) and reports, per histogram: non-monotonic cumulative buckets; `le="+Inf"` disagreeing with `_count`; `le` labels that do not parse as a float (`le="NaN"` is storable today); duplicate `le` spellings carrying different values at the same timestamp (`le="1"` vs `le="1.0"` on disjoint timestamps — the v3 migration shape — is recognized as clean); histograms with no `+Inf` bucket at all. Exits non-zero when anything is found, so it can run from cron or CI. Placed under `promtool tsdb` because it takes a database path like `dump` and `analyze` (`promtool check` takes config files and server URLs), and marked `[Experimental]` like `dump-openmetrics`. **Limits.** Native histograms are out of scope — already validated at append. And I have not measured how often such data occurs in the wild — this tool is how an operator answers that for their own TSDB. Found and verified on `main` at `44d6a0e`; file and line references are against that commit. cc @dgl — promtool is your path, and this proposes a new subcommand in it.

signal.title: otlptranslator: keep le="+Inf" equal to count when a bound is +Inf
signal.text: Previously, an OTLP histogram whose `explicit_bounds` end at `+Inf` produced two `le="+Inf"` samples for the same series and timestamp: one from the loop over explicit bounds, carrying the cumulative count at that bound, and one synthesized from `pt.Count()`. Both appends succeed, because a duplicate at the same timestamp is rejected across appender batches and not within one, and the commit keeps the first. So `le="+Inf"` ended up holding a bucket total while `_count` held the count. This skips an infinite bound in the loop and lets the synthesized bucket carry the count: ```go if math.IsInf(bound, 1) { continue } ``` `explicit_bounds` is required to be strictly increasing, so in conforming input `+Inf` is the last bound and no later bucket depends on the skipped iteration. The bound's exemplars still reach the synthesized bucket through the remainder assigned after the loop, so no exemplar is dropped. No existing fixture in the package sets an infinite bound, so the guard does not change any current output. The NHCB path already refuses the same input: `histogram.Validate()` rejects an explicitly defined `+Inf` bound at `model/histogram/generic.go:566`, and #17320 kept that while relaxing `-Inf`. This brings the classic path into line with it. `TestPrometheusConverter_ExplicitInfBoundDoesNotReplaceCount` fails on `main` with `le="+Inf" was written more than once` and passes with the change. #### Which issue(s) does the PR fix: Fixes #19424 #### Release notes for end users (**ALL** commits must be considered). *Reviewers should verify clarity and quality.* ```release-notes [BUGFIX] OTLP: Keep `le="+Inf"` equal to the data point count when explicit bounds end at `+Inf`. ```

signal.title: otlptranslator: valid OTLP histogram stored with le="+Inf" below its own _count
signal.text: ### What did you do? On `main` at `44d6a0e0b`, translated a classic `HistogramDataPoint` whose explicit bounds end at `+Inf`, then read back its series: ```go pt.SetCount(42) pt.SetSum(100) pt.BucketCounts().FromRaw([]uint64{5, 10, 20, 7}) pt.ExplicitBounds().FromRaw([]float64{1, 2, math.Inf(1)}) ``` This data point satisfies every MUST the proto states for it: `bucket_counts` is one longer than `explicit_bounds`, the bounds are strictly increasing, and `count` equals their sum (`5 + 10 + 20 + 7 = 42`). ### What did you expect to see? `le="+Inf"` equal to `_count`, as the cumulative convention requires. ### What did you see instead? Under which circumstances? Two totals, disagreeing. `_count` is `42` and `le="+Inf"` is `35`, so the stored histogram answers differently depending on which series is read, and nothing reports it: the input broke no MUST, the bucket series is still monotonic, and no error is returned. **The same input is rejected on the other path.** With `convert_histograms_to_nhcb: true` the identical data point becomes ``` {count:42, sum:100, [-Inf,1]:5, (1,2]:10, (2,+Inf]:20, (+Inf,+Inf]:7} ``` and `histogram.Validate()` refuses it: ``` custom buckets: last +Inf bound must not be explicitly defined: histogram custom bounds must be finite ``` That rule is `model/histogram/generic.go:566`, and `tsdb/head_append.go:828` turns it into a rejected sample. It also looks deliberate rather than incidental: #17320 revisited that function to accept `-Inf` and kept `+Inf` rejected. So the invariant is already stated here, an explicit `+Inf` bound must not be defined, and the classic path is the one that does not hold to it — while being the default, since `convert_histograms_to_nhcb` is absent from `DefaultOTLPConfig`. **Where the second `le="+Inf"` comes from.** The loop over explicit bounds writes one `_bucket` series per bound, formatting the bound into `le` (`helper.go:308-337`), so the `+Inf` bound emits `le="+Inf"` carrying the cumulative count at that point, `35`. Then `le="+Inf"` is synthesized again from `pt.Count()` (`helper.go:340-346`). Both reach `Append` with identical labels and timestamp. Both are accepted and the commit keeps the first: two appends of `35` then `42` at the same timestamp in one batch return no error and store `35`, while the same second append issued after a commit is refused with `duplicate sample for timestamp 1000; overrides not allowed: existing 35, new value 99`. The fourth bucket count, `7`, is the overflow bucket, which this path never reads. **A test that shows it.** Fails on `main`, passes with the change: ``` --- FAIL: TestPrometheusConverter_ExplicitInfBoundDoesNotReplaceCount (0.00s) Messages: le="+Inf" was written more than once ``` **How often this happens — my guess is rarely, and here is the reasoning.** I have not counted producers. The schema makes an explicit `+Inf` bound unnecessary: `bucket_counts` must be one longer than `explicit_bounds`, so the last count already means "above the last bound". An SDK following that shape has no reason to emit one, which leaves translators from formats where `+Inf` is explicit, a Prometheus classic histogram round-tripping through OTLP being the obvious case. So I would expect this to be uncommon. It still seemed worth reporting, because the input is valid, the loss is silent, and the guard is one condition. A PR follows with the change and the test above. /cc @beorn7, who kept the explicit `+Inf` bound rejected in #17320, and @ArthurSens for `otlptranslator`. ### Prometheus version ```text prometheus, version (branch: main, revision: 44d6a0e0b1dbdcba4e68853d50e0bafc87d90507) build user: build date: go version: go1.26.1 platform: darwin/arm64 tags: unknown ```

signal.title: Avoid locking HEAD shards when running gc
signal.text: After HEAD writes a block it runs GC to prune series that no longer have any chunks in HEAD, this fully locks each HEAD shard while it's being scanned for series to prune. That locked shard blocks all queries (because it's a write lock) and it can be visible on metrics as a sudden spike in queued queries. The more series we have in Prometheus the more visible this is. Often there are very few series to actually prune, so most of this time is spent iterating over all series, the more series the longer each shard scan takes (since the number of shards is static). Try to avoid this blocking by doing prunes in two phases: - first iterate under a read lock and find series to prune - then, if there are any series found, do a second loop over identified series and prune these under a write lock This way we only lock each shard to the actual pruning, not for scanning. It's safe because series can only receive samples, they can't become empty, while we're running a GC. <!-- - Please give your PR a title in the form "area: short description". signal.title: scrape: synthesize start times for summary _sum and _count series
signal.text: Motivation: Start-timestamp (ST) auto-synthesis was implemented for all cumulative counter-like series on the scrape path, but summary types were left out: their _sum and _count series (which have counter semantics) did not get a synthesized start time. This was tracked by an in-code TODO and called out by maintainers as the remaining gap for #14763. Approach: Extend checkAndSynthesizeStartTime to handle model.MetricTypeSummary. A summary family exposes cumulative _sum and _count series alongside gauge-like quantile series, so only the _sum and _count series may be synthesized. The quantile series (whose metric name equals the metric family name) are deliberately excluded so their gauge values are never run through counter reset-detection. Suffix matching mirrors the existing isSeriesPartOfFamily logic and is allocation-free. The stCache doc comment is updated to reflect the newly supported series. Validation: go test ./scrape/ -run 'TestScrapeLoopAppend_StartTimeSynthesis' -race -count=1 Passes, including the new TestScrapeLoopAppend_StartTimeSynthesis_Summary, which asserts that _sum/_count get deltas with a synthesized ST (anchor and reset paths) while the quantile series keep ST=0. ```release-notes [ENHANCEMENT] Scrape: Synthesize start timestamps for summary `_sum` and `_count` series when start-time synthesis is enabled. ``` Fixes #14763 Signed-off-by: Pujitha Paladugu <10557236+pujitha24@users.noreply.github.com>
